newsitem.title: USA: INTERVIEW - Kodak to cut U.S. film prices - CFO. [CORRECTED 21:36 GMT]
newsitem.headline: INTERVIEW - Kodak to cut U.S. film prices - CFO. [CORRECTED 21:36 GMT]

text.p: Eastman Kodak Co, enmeshed in a price war with Fuji Photo Film Co and other competitors, could cut some U.S. film prices this year. Kodak Chief Financial Officer Harry Kavetas, when asked in an interview with Reuters whether such price cuts would occur, said, "I would sure expect so."
Kavetas said that some products could be affected by cuts of more than five percent but that the main line consumer film business will not be affected that much.
(Corrects to make clear that Kodak CFO was not referring to the company's main line consumer film business when he said there could be price cuts of five percent or more.)
"We have no interest in losing market share," Kavetas said on Wednesday. "We'll take that kind of action if we have to."
Merrill Lynch analyst Robert Curran said Kodak had about two-thirds of the U.S. film market.

How much the company will cut its prices depends "a lot on what the other players do, including our competitors," Kavetas said. The reductions could exceed five percent by year's end, depending on the product, he added.

The price cuts could boost Kodak's revenue by enabling the company -- ideally -- to sell more film, Kavetas said, without specifying when the cuts would occur. That would in turn could increase the company's U.S. market share, he said.

By some analysts' estimates, Kodak has lost as much as a five percent share of the U.S. film market since the beginning of the year. According to Kavetas, however, the company has only lost between 1.0 and 2.0 percent in the last 12 months.

Earlier Wednesday, Kodak posted second-quarter earnings of $1.12 a share, below the First Call consensus estimate of $1.39 a share and less than the $1.30 a share Kodak earned in the second quarter of last year.
Kodak said the results were hurt by film pricing pressures, as well as higher losses for its digital products and increased marketing expenses for its new Advantix camera system.
After an opening delay, the company's shares plunged more than nine points to around 67. By early afternoon, they stood at 68-7/8, down 8.
U.S. film price cuts, however, "aren't the only tool we have in our toolbox," Kavetas added.
"As opposed to a knee-jerk reaction with price cuts, we have to be sure we have leading products to put into the marketplace and use that as leverage," Kavetas said.
The products, including some of the company's new camera systems such as Advantix, will continue to be backed by increased marketing expenditures, Kavetas also said.
"We have a series of programs in play that are very important," he said.
Kavetas said Kodak would spend a "considerable amount of money" on marketing Advantix, although did not specify the amount.
Kodak will also increase its collaboration with the retailers of Advantix and other products, he added.
Last month, in a move to invigorate marketing efforts, the company consolidated its advertising accounts with Oglivy & Mather Worldwide, a unit of Britain's WPP Group Plc.
